name: What to Do When Someone Dies Checklist
description: A step-by-step US checklist for the hours, weeks and months after a loved one dies, ordered by what needs to happen first.

items.text: Get a legal pronouncement of death
items.note: If the person was in hospice, call the hospice team. If the death was unexpected at home, call 911. In a hospital or care facility, staff will handle it.

items.text: Tell close family and friends, and ask one person to help spread the news
Check for written funeral wishes or a prepaid funeral plan
Contact a funeral home to transport the body
Lock the home, secure valuables and car keys, and stop mail if no one lives there
Arrange care for pets and any dependents
Ask the funeral home for its itemized price list before you choose services
items.note: Federal law requires funeral homes to give you this list, and you can buy a casket or urn elsewhere.

items.text: Plan the funeral, burial, cremation or memorial service
If the person served in the military, ask about VA burial benefits at VA.gov
Write and publish an obituary
Notify the person's employer and ask about final pay, life insurance and retirement benefits
Order several certified copies of the death certificate
items.note: The funeral home can usually order them for you. Many agencies accept only certified copies, not photocopies.

items.text: Find the will, trust documents and any letter of wishes
Gather the person's Social Security number, birth certificate, marriage certificate and military discharge papers
Collect recent bank statements, bills and insurance policies
Confirm the funeral home reported the death to Social Security
Ask Social Security about survivor benefits and the one-time death payment
items.note: Social Security doesn't pay benefits for the month of death. A payment that arrives after the death may have to be returned, so don't spend it until you check.

items.text: Notify the VA if the person received veterans benefits
Cancel the driver's license or state ID with the DMV
Forward mail with the post office if needed
Contact each bank and credit card company the person used
Ask Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to flag the credit report as deceased
items.note: This helps prevent identity theft, which often targets people who have recently died. Each bureau will ask for a copy of the death certificate.

items.text: File claims with life insurance companies and pension plans
Cancel subscriptions, phone plans, streaming services and memberships
Close or memorialize email and social media accounts
Keep paying home insurance and utilities on any property until it is sold or transferred
Give the original will to the executor
Check with the county probate court whether probate is needed
items.note: Many states let small estates skip full probate. The court clerk can explain your options but can't give legal advice.

items.text: Get an employer identification number (EIN) from the IRS if the estate needs its own bank account
Make a list of the estate's assets and debts
File the person's final federal and state income tax returns
items.note: The final return covers January 1 to the date of death and is due on the usual tax deadline the following year. A surviving spouse can usually file jointly for that year.

items.text: Ask a tax professional whether the estate must file its own income tax return
Search for unclaimed money in each state where the person lived at unclaimed.org
Update your own will and beneficiary forms if the person was named in them
Give yourself time to grieve, and reach out for grief support if you need it

faq.q: How many death certificates do I need?
faq.a: Many families order several certified copies, often 5 to 10, because banks, insurers, pension plans and government agencies may each ask for one. Count the accounts and policies you know about and add a few extra. You can order more later from the state or county vital records office, but it takes time.

faq.q: Who notifies Social Security when someone dies?
faq.a: The funeral home usually reports the death to Social Security if you give them the person's Social Security number. You can't report a death online. To ask about survivor benefits, call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 or contact your local office.

faq.q: Am I responsible for a family member's debts after they die?
faq.a: Usually not. Debts are paid from the person's estate. You are generally only responsible if you co-signed, shared the account, or live in a community property state where different rules can apply. Don't pay a debt from your own money until you know you owe it.

faq.q: Do you have to go through probate?
faq.a: Not always. Assets with a named beneficiary, jointly owned property and assets held in a trust usually pass without probate. Many states also have a simpler process for small estates. If the person owned property in their own name only, the executor may need to open probate in the county where they lived.
